questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}+4x+10$ and the point $P(0,10)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(10,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,10).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}+4x+10 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{2}{3}x+4 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =4\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(0,10)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(10,0)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(10) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(10))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1).$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(0).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(0)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(0) & =x \\ f(x) & =0 \\ (x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1) & =0 \\ x & =-2,\,0.\end{aligned}
$$

We discard $x=-2$ since the logarithm is not defined for negative numbers. Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(0)=0.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{2(x+2)}{2x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 0+1)+\frac{2(0+2)}{2\cdot 0+1} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =0+4 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={x}^{3}+2x+1.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(1).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(1),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(1).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(1)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(1) & =x \\ f(x) & =1 \\ {x}^{3}+2x+1 & =1 \\ x({x}^{2}+2) & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(1)=0.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{3}+2x+1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+2 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\cdot 0+2 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and the point $P(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\pi }{6})$ is$\,${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\pi }{6})$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
